quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Before mixing two-part epoxy or polyester resin with fiberglass or carbon fiber reinforcement for Composite Materials Requirement 1, what safety precautions are mandatory?
quiz_item.question: Before mixing two-part epoxy or polyester resin with fiberglass or carbon fiber reinforcement for Composite Materials Requirement 1, what safety precautions are mandatory?
options: A. Mix large batches of resin and catalyst in a tall, narrow plastic cup inside an unventilated closet and handle cut glass fibers with bare hands.

B. Read the Safety Data Sheets (SDS) for all resins and hardeners, work in a well-ventilated area, wear chemical-resistant nitrile gloves, safety goggles, long sleeves, and an appropriate dust mask/respirator, and mix small batches in shallow containers to prevent runaway exothermic heat.
C. Heat the hardener catalyst over an open flame to speed up curing and blow fiberglass sanding dust across the room with compressed air.
D. Wash uncured epoxy resin off bare skin using acetone or lacquer thinner so the solvent carries the chemicals deeper into your pores.

pamphlet_excerpts: Covering Large Project Surfaces: In large composites projects, several pieces of fiberglass reinforcement might be necessary to cover the surface (p. 60).
Overlapping Fiberglass Seams Properly: When you join pieces of fiberglass reinforcement to form a seam, overlap the pieces by 1 to 3 inches (p. 60).
Preserving Structural Laminate Strength: This ensures that the structural properties of the laminate are not weakened (p. 60).
Staggering Multi-Layer Overlaps: If you use more than one layer of reinforcement, be sure to stagger or space out the overlaps to avoid thick buildups that also can create weak areas (p. 60).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Maintain Seam Overlap Strength: This ensures that the structural properties of the laminate are not weakened (p. 60).

Step 2 - Stagger Multi-Layer Seam Overlaps: If you use more than one layer of reinforcement, be sure to stagger or space out the overlaps to avoid thick buildups that also can create weak areas (p. 60).
Step 3 - Eliminate Trapped Air Pockets: When you saturate the fiberglass reinforcement with resin, air can be trapped in the laminate, creating voids (p. 60).
Step 4 - Inspect Cured Laminate for Voids: Air voids are simply bubbles, which when trapped in the cured laminate can cause problems ranging from poor appearance to structural failure (p. 60).
